recommendation: test-first: one authors' measurement, a second paper only argues it; add after clean-trace training and check held-out recovery.

what_and_how: Choose the harness first and keep it in place during post-training, so the model trains on the states that harness produces. After a harness change that lowers return, keep training the same weights under the new harness.
problem: A harness added after training recovers little of the benefit of training with it.
best_number: training-time beats post-hoc by 20.7 points (h-mid) and 22.5 points (h-high) (2606.25447)
verdict: survived: Training a small model with the harness in the loop beats training outside it.
recommendation: build-in-regime: only when you train weights, and then for small models.

what_and_how: Change the harness between training samples: rename and rewrite skills and tools, reorder prompt rules, give each task a different configuration (an anchor plus its nearest neighbours, or an orthogonal subset), and share trajectories across harness versions. The model learns function, not surface form.
problem: A model trained under one harness breaks when its prompt or tool names change.
best_number: Qwen3-4B-Instruct: ClawGym-Bench in-space 52.78 vs 50.46 for random assignment (Table 3) (2610.29458)
verdict: survived: Training across varied harnesses transfers better than training on one fixed harness.
recommendation: build-in-regime: verdict survived with medium evidence, but it matters only if you train small models.

what_and_how: Keep a small window of active harnesses or stages. Every fixed number of steps score each on a short eval, retire any that pass a mastery threshold, and refill from unlearned ones near a learnable pass rate. Mix in replay of earlier data and variants with cues removed.
problem: Training on one harness or stage at a time forgets earlier skills and overfits fixed prompts.
best_number: held-out parallel rate 89% (CHART-3) vs at most 5% for fixed pools (2609.22247)
novelty: novel: rotate a small window of training harnesses, retiring each at measured mastery.
verdict: not judged
recommendation: test-first: single model, mostly one run, own benchmark and a narrow behaviour (parallel search); small-model training only.

what_and_how: In group-relative reinforcement learning, count each rollout once: compute the group baseline over rollouts and pool tokens per rollout, however many training samples its calls produced. Drop groups whose rollouts all score the same before normalizing.
problem: Multi-call agents give long rollouts extra weight, and uniform groups add noise.
best_number: 38.2% at step 128, compared with 35.0% for the baseline (2608.17528)
verdict: not judged
recommendation: test-first: authors' gain of about three points at one step count; low cost when training.

what_and_how: Run several rollouts per task and keep only tasks solved sometimes (for example one to three of four). Keep a bounded window of current failures that retires solved tasks, keep only failures adding a new mechanism, and order tasks by difficulty.
problem: Tasks always solved or never solved give no learning signal.
best_number: gpt-oss-20b: 36.0 vs 28.0 with window size 1 (BrowseComp-Plus) (2609.26760)
verdict: not judged
recommendation: test-first: authors' ablations on small task counts; cheap to build.

what_and_how: Shape the training reward beyond pass or fail: credit each step by its gain over same-state alternatives and pass later gains back to the steps that enabled them, reward the fraction of checks passed (zero if any old test breaks), and normalize tool and reply segments separately.
problem: A single end-of-episode reward says little about which step mattered.
best_number: Qwen2.5-3B (Table 3): 2Wiki F1 65.53 full vs 63.42 without enablement term (2607.27652)
verdict: not judged
recommendation: test-first: authors' ablations of two to three points, no repeats stated; only relevant if you train weights.

what_and_how: Pay only the rubric score at the end of the episode, with zero potentials in the shaping formula. No bonus for checking, revising or any other operation, so the model finds its own process.
problem: Action bonuses train the model to perform the rewarded motions instead of solving the task.
best_number: none
verdict: not judged
recommendation: test-first: argued only, no result in the line; compare against step credit on your own task before choosing.

what_and_how: Train only a small set of added or selected parameters: a rank-32 or rank-64 adapter on projections, a rank-8 shift added after each block, two normalization scale sets chosen by subtask type, or gradient routing of action and argument tokens to chosen units. Base weights stay frozen.
problem: Full fine-tuning of small models is costly and can erase general ability.
models: Kimi K2.7 Code, Qwen3.5-2B, Qwen3-8B, Qwen2.5-3B
best_number: DeepSWE 31.0→43.4; no full fine-tune comparison (2610.00890)
verdict: not judged
recommendation: test-first: all gains are authors' own and none compared against full fine-tuning; low risk when training small local models.

what_and_how: Train one model on several prompt views of the same episodes (history to action, history plus document to action, history to document) in one summed loss, alternating batches from each view instead of finishing one view first.
problem: Single-view training loses supervision that the other views carry.
best_number: 22.98 task success with all three views vs 20.58 with the replay view alone (2610.20261)
verdict: not judged
recommendation: test-first: one paper, a two-point gain on one model; skip unless you train small models.

what_and_how: Build training or evaluation tasks from real cases in stages (contract, scenario, blueprint, executable environment with verifier), with a code gate after each stage. Roll out an open model to test difficulty, patch failures within a bounded repair budget, and send the rest to humans.
problem: Hand-written benchmarks are scarce, and generated tasks are often unsolvable or leaky.
best_number: 547 candidates, 315 runnable, 281 kept (2611.03698)
verdict: not judged
recommendation: test-first: built in nine papers but none measured against a baseline; audit each task with a reference solution.

what_and_how: Derive a problem statement and requirements from original code and selected tests, then remove those tests from the task package. Give the builder only interface stubs, and build the test mask by uniting validated scopes of compatible test files.
problem: Agents that see the tests overfit them, and unscoped tests reward unrelated code.
best_number: none
verdict: not judged
recommendation: test-first: argued, nothing measured; use when building acceptance tests for a multi-role code pipeline and check that hidden tests still discriminate.

pattern: Staged filter funnel over mined cases
what_and_how: Fetch frozen snapshots of public issues or repositories, then filter in separate logged stages (label, reactions, length, bug type, comment cap, deduplication, model labelling with quoted evidence), pick the densest period, and cap text per case.
problem: Raw mined data is noisy, and one-step filtering hides what was dropped.
best_number: DeepSeek V4.1 Flash: 4,222 false and 25 unclear labels of 40,901 repositories (2611.15436)
verdict: not judged
recommendation: test-first: no baseline measurement; per-stage counts are the audit trail; use for building case sets, not at run time.

what_and_how: Order repairs by cost: fixed rules and cached fixes first, then a capped number of model proposals (seven per project) accepted only after replay. Pick actions from typed error kinds, use regular expressions last with the safe action, and on retrieval failure fall back to keyword search and log once.
problem: Model calls for routine repairs cost money and vary, and silent degradation hides failures.
best_number: GLM 5.3; 306 of 729 projects (42.0%) met the acceptance criteria (2610.33851)
verdict: survived: Moving repeated steps from model calls into fixed code or batched calls cuts cost or latency about 10 to 25 times at the same success.
recommendation: test-first: verdict survived but evidence weak, authors' own systems; cheap and fits any harness; measure cost before and after.

what_and_how: Run the unmodified harness in a container behind a proxy that logs every model and system call to a database, tags calls by component, and applies hooks that rewrite context or tool arguments. Turn traces into steps with data-flow edges and mark model-dependent code by taint analysis.
problem: Without step-level records, failures and cost cannot be attributed to one component.
best_number: Claude Code with Haiku 5.5: mean cost change −1.50%, 95% interval [−4.69%, +2.04%] (2611.12122)
verdict: not judged
recommendation: test-first: infrastructure with no gain claim, the one measured effect is a null cost change; build the logging as plumbing anyway.

what_and_how: Label every failure as an interaction edge between two components plus a fault side, the component whose repair it calls for. When several errors contribute, label the earliest failure after which the run never recovers. Keep only episode boundaries that two independent model calls agree on.
problem: Failure reports blame the wrong component, so fixes miss the cause.
best_number: GPT-5.5 category kappa 0.76 against the human annotator (Figure 3) (2607.28802)
verdict: not judged
recommendation: test-first: labelling schemes agreed with one human annotator, no effect on repairs measured; useful for reading failures from a multi-role code pipeline.

pattern: Route by model and harness vectors
what_and_how: Learn a vector per model and per harness from pooled outcomes. Score a query by each component's match plus a three-way term, so harness preference can change with the model. Give unobserved components zero vectors with their text description, and pick one pair per query minus cost.
problem: Choosing a model and harness pair by hand misses pairings never tried.
best_number: 73.93 mean routing accuracy vs 66.65 for IrtNet (Table 1) (2609.32213)
novelty: novel: learned per-query choice of model and harness pair, including never-run pairs.
verdict: contested: Routing steps or sessions to cheaper models is reported to save 13 to 90 percent, but per-request switching can break the prompt cache.
recommendation: test-first: scored on recorded outcomes, not live runs; cache effects untested.

what_and_how: Profile each configuration offline on latency, throughput and quality. Per agent role or workload regime, pick the configuration with the shortest run time that passes quality and stability checks, fixed before testing. Add a dispatch rule only when profiles show a distinct limiter.
problem: One inference setting wastes time or capacity across roles with different loads.
best_number: GLM-4.7-Flash: 1.23× (BrowseComp-Plus), 2.45× (DeepResearchBench) end-to-end (2610.06597)
verdict: not judged
recommendation: test-first: two papers, one on agent roles and one on kernels; matters only when self-hosting several roles.

pattern: Operator policy levers read by code
what_and_how: Operators set value priorities, source authority, never-rules, review triggers, maturity thresholds that rise with action risk, and verification depth scaled by criticality as settings. The gate reads them and the model cannot change them.
problem: Policy stated in a prompt can be ignored or argued away by the model.
best_number: violations up to 100% of environments above 2.67 times policy authority without oversight (2610.16015)
verdict: survived: Deterministic checks outside the model, such as capability scope, provenance and a per-action policy gate, block attacks at near-zero benign refusals.
recommendation: build: verdict survived with medium evidence for code-owned gates; these lines argue or use scripted oracles.

pattern: Keep unknown visible, reject bad input
what_and_how: Give reachability three states (reached, unreached, unresolved) and keep unresolved code in scope at lower priority and in the report. Reject observed values above a bound, beyond a rounding allowance, instead of silently capping them.
problem: Silent drops and clipping let a harness treat unknown or invalid as safe.
best_number: none
verdict: not judged
recommendation: test-first: nothing measured in these lines; cheap rules.

what_and_how: Let the model produce raw estimates or factors, then correct them in code: a least-absolute-deviations line fitted on labelled items, a regressor mapping scores and confidence to a rounded item score, a likelihood-ratio product turned into a probability, or a shrunk recent-ratio correction.
problem: Model estimates are biased, and asking the model to correct itself fails.
best_number: GPT-5.4: Brier 0.0764 full vs 0.0815 narrative and 0.0807 probability-space (Table 5) (2609.05905)
verdict: not judged
recommendation: test-first: four papers by their own authors, each on a narrow domain, and labelled items are needed.

what_and_how: Give the model a folder of documentation, a few starter tools and a terminal, or run a base model through the raw completion interface, or grow from an empty program with no controller. The model picks its own workflow and no solutions carry between episodes.
problem: Prescribed workflows can cut capability and hide what the model can do alone.
best_number: Claude Code with Opus 5: 99.0% CaP-Bench, 87.0% LIBERO-PRO (2610.02459)
verdict: survived: In open-ended diagnosis and engineering tasks, prescribed multi-role or fixed-step agents lose to a simple harness that lets the model choose its own calls.
recommendation: build-in-regime: survived at medium evidence for strong models on open-ended work; no ablation here and not for small models.

what_and_how: Run the same model under two or more harnesses (a frontier coding harness and an open one, or each model in its own harness) so harness and model effects separate on matched pairs. Report each pairing.
problem: A score blends model and harness, so a harness change cannot be judged.
best_number: Claude-Opus-5 alignment down 15.2%, GPT-5.6-Sol down 24.0% (Expert Nitpicker) (2610.13022)
verdict: survived: No single harness wins everywhere: the best harness changes with the model and the benchmark, so test model and harness as a pair.
recommendation: build: verdict survived with medium evidence and it is cheap; run your harness against a stock one on each model.

what_and_how: Repair generated 3D scenes with code: convex parts for collision meshes, a support graph from bounding boxes, gravity settling until speeds drop, smallest-movement overlap removal within a budget, and anchor-only point fusion across edit rounds.
problem: Generated scenes float, interpenetrate or leave gaps, so a robot simulation fails.
best_number: stable rest 8/12 with settling and separation against 1/12 without (2610.17651)
verdict: not judged
recommendation: test-first: specific to scene generation.

what_and_how: A program or simulator holds world state and rules, and checks pass first. A video model then adds appearance, conditioned on the verified proxy render, a reference frame and a prompt. Vary parameters and keep only verified videos as training pairs.
problem: Video models ignore physics, and checking pixels cannot verify motion.
best_number: GPT-6 Astra with Seedance 2.5 refiner: generation 85.00 versus 80.00 without refiner; repair 86.00 versus 60.67; realism 3.72 versus 2.59 (2611.16748)
novelty: novel: code-held verified state first; the model renders appearance only.
verdict: not judged
recommendation: test-first: authors' gains on 100 tasks, no repeats stated; unrelated to a harness that handles text only, though verifying in code before model polish transfers.

what_and_how: Separate environment workers (reusable simulator slots), rollout workers that batch model requests by compatibility, and a gateway with a session registry. Run one remote container per rollout, created and deleted outside the training nodes.
problem: Training agent policies is bottlenecked by environment and inference latency.
best_number: 53% lower average inference latency (2608.16590)
verdict: not judged
recommendation: test-first: only matters when training agents; one measurement with the model not stated.

what_and_how: On development tasks measure the noise floor, delivery rate, plan quality among delivered plans and failure shares. Rule: below about 0.18 delivered quality the harness lever paid nothing; loops dominant means evolve the harness; saturated delivery with planning failures means train weights.
problem: Teams pick harness work or weight training by habit, not measurement.
best_number: none
novelty: novel: measured decision rule choosing between harness evolution and weight training.
verdict: not judged
recommendation: test-first: argued in this line with no result; thresholds came from one planning benchmark.

what_and_how: Package each reusable resource (tool, code part, proof method) with a resident model that applies it in context to natural-language requests and calls other primitives. Give each an application scope (when it helps or hurts) and a contract of inputs, outputs, environment needs and dependencies.
problem: Raw tools and skills carry no guidance on when they apply, so agents misuse or skip them.
best_number: Claude Opus 5.5 with Claude Code 9 of 46 tasks alone, 39 with HEELO (2611.07461)
novelty: novel: each reusable primitive carries its own resident model that applies it.
verdict: not judged
recommendation: test-first: headline is the authors' own, and the paper reports only 1.2 to 1.5 points over strong baselines on one benchmark; try on one tool family.

what_and_how: Ship each extension behind a flag resolved by runtime override, build flag, environment variable, then default off. Disable a failed extension and log it. Run a legacy script as a black-box subprocess beside the agent engine behind one flag, and install controls from one package manifest.
problem: Adding agent behaviour to a live system risks breaking what already works.
best_number: gpt-5.4-nano: baseline 15/89, round B 17/89 (2604.20938)
verdict: not judged
recommendation: test-first: a two-task measured change, the safety value is argued.

what_and_how: Build a graph of required edits from repository dependency and change-impact links (a unit follows another when it edits the same hunk or imports, calls or subclasses what it introduced; skip hot files and lockfiles), then derive each next step from it.
problem: Multi-file changes fail when the agent edits in the wrong order or misses dependents.
best_number: none
verdict: not judged
recommendation: test-first: argued only; fits code-change work such as producing a code change for review; test against a plain plan.

what_and_how: Before any tool call the model, or a human, writes a short step plan; the plan is placed in context and the agent follows it, sometimes with a reflection prompt later. Keep it brief and tied to budgets.
problem: Agents act without structure and drift or waste steps on multi-step tasks.
best_number: Qwen 3 14B plan +10.87, reflection +5.19, both +12.45; o4-mini +0.17 to +1.10 (Table 2) (2603.08877)
verdict: survived: A written plan or planning step lifts weaker or mid-tier models by roughly 6 to 12 points on coding, retail and web tasks.
recommendation: build-in-regime: gain shows on weaker or mid-tier models, flat on strong ones.

pattern: Stronger model plans for weaker executor
what_and_how: A stronger model writes one plan in a plan-only first turn (at most eight steps) and hands it to the cheaper executor before its first edit; executor, scaffold and turn limit stay fixed.
problem: A cheap executor plans poorly, and a plan from the same model adds little.
best_number: Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct; no plan 42.8, self-plan 48.2, Qwen3-Coder-480B-A35B-Instruct planner 49.2, Claude Sonnet 4.5 planner 57.8 (2608.06113)
verdict: survived: One plan from a stronger model, handed to a weaker executor before its first edit, lifts success by many points.
recommendation: build: two benchmarks with matched budgets and no-plan controls.

what_and_how: Give the agent a plan tool (update_plan or todo_write) that replaces the whole list, allow one item in progress, check format, and print the current plan into every turn instead of stored history. A markdown task tree works the same way.
problem: Agents lose track of finished and open steps in long runs.
best_number: Nemotron-3 30B SWE-Bench: planning increases success rate by 11.6 percentage points (2609.20804)
verdict: survived: A persistent, structured plan or state object the agent sees every turn beats prose notes or none for mid-tier models; fails to help some backbones.
recommendation: test-first: evidence weak, authors' own harnesses, one backbone showed no change; try for small local models and keep it only if it moves the score.

what_and_how: After each subtask or worker handoff, check success; on failure the planner rewrites only the remaining pending steps from the current state, or a diagnosis step repairs the unsupported part of the plan. Cap replans, keep finished steps fixed.
problem: A plan fixed before execution breaks when the environment or a step result differs.
verdict: survived: A plan fixed before execution loses to a plan revised from execution results, test results or failure diagnosis; removing replanning costs several points.
recommendation: test-first: evidence weak, authors' own ablations on one model each; cheap to add in a code-change pipeline, keep it only after a held-out check.

what_and_how: A planner turns the request into an ordered list of at most six bounded subtasks, each with a checkable completion criterion; each subtask runs its own loop and returns a compact answer; split along natural boundaries such as clusters or intents.
problem: One long prompt overloads the model and hides which part failed.
models: Gemini-3.1 Pro, GLM-5.2, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, Gemini 2.5 Pro
best_number: Gemini-3.1 Pro: 60% without subtask planning versus 96% default (Figure 9 labels) (2609.10522)
verdict: survived: On tasks the bare model rarely completes, staged decomposition with validation and feedback raises success by tens of points; on atomic steps it adds little.
recommendation: build-in-regime: only where the bare model often fails; skip on atomic steps.

what_and_how: The planner emits tasks with explicit dependencies; the harness checks references, rejects cycles, runs each wave of ready tasks in parallel, passes outputs to consumers, cancels descendants of a failed task, and retries a failed section alone.
problem: Serial plans waste time and cannot show which step feeds which.
best_number: gpt-oss-120b: 41.3% to 58.0% BrowseComp-Plus accuracy, planning and state off to on (Table 11) (2610.15208)
verdict: survived: Organising skills or tasks by an explicit stage plan or dependency graph beats a flat set; parallel running is argued, not measured.
recommendation: test-first: gains measured by authors on own benchmarks; parallel speedup argued.

what_and_how: Split the job into fixed ordered stages (usage notes, snippets, assembly, final pass; or preprocess, navigate, extract, review), each with its own prompt and a check before the next stage; later stages read earlier output.
problem: A single free-form run skips steps and varies between runs.
models: gpt-5.4, GPT-5.5 + Codex, Qwen3-32B, Seed2.0 Lite
verdict: survived: Fixed pipelines with admission gates give more consistently successful and more stable runs than one plain call or a bare agent.
recommendation: test-first: evidence weak, authors' own pipelines; measure against a plain agent loop on your tasks.

pattern: Code checks the plan before execution
what_and_how: The model proposes a plan or route as structured data; code validates it against a schema, state graph or physical rules, rejects violations and re-prompts up to two times; each step can also be checked against rules before running.
problem: Model plans contain invalid steps that only fail at execution.
best_number: GPT-5.5 and GPT-6-Astra, all 32 tasks: Model + Skills plus route harness collision avoidance 76.9 and 80.0 versus 43.8 and 34.4 (Table 4, page 8) (2609.20822)
verdict: survived: Where the domain has explicit state and rules, moving plan checking and repair into deterministic code beats model feedback loops and lifts small models.
recommendation: build-in-regime: only where state and rules are explicit and checkable.

what_and_how: Before touching the environment, roll the candidate plan, route or edit through a model of the program or scene (search over rollouts, call-graph path walk, translucent preview with feasibility report) and act only on a passing one.
problem: Real actions are costly or irreversible and failures show up too late.
models: Claude Opus 4.8, MiniMax-M3, GPT-5.6-Luna, Claude Haiku-4.5
best_number: Claude Opus 4.8; relative human action efficiency 72.9% full vs 59.2% without planning (Table 1) (2609.39140)
verdict: not judged
recommendation: test-first: measured only by own authors on narrow tasks, no verdict; try where a dry run is cheap.

what_and_how: The model first writes a requirement document or task contract (acceptance criteria, assumptions, open items, preservation obligations) from the request, then a design, and implements against it; a second pass drops unsupported requirements.
problem: Coding from the raw request guesses requirements and misses constraints.
models: GPT-5.6-Sol, Claude Opus 4.6, Claude Sonnet 4.6, DeepSeek-V4-Pro
best_number: GPT-5.6-Sol via Codex: GameCraft-Bench 0.012 to 0.273; MiniAppBench 0.451 to 0.543; WebGen-Bench 0.271 to 0.384 (2610.13022)
verdict: survived: Writing a requirement or specification document before coding, and stating what must be preserved, raises success where the bare model does badly.
recommendation: build-in-regime: gains where the bare model does badly, compact bounded code can do better without it.

what_and_how: Before solving, the model fills a typed artifact: formulation sets and variables, a decision table of rules, a quantitative baseline with assumptions, or a hierarchy of nodes; the model edits it during work and it feeds later steps.
problem: Free text reasoning leaves rules and assumptions implicit and unchecked.
models: Qwen3.5-4B, GPT-5.4, DeepSeek v4.1 Flash, claude-opus-4-7
verdict: not judged
recommendation: test-first: measured only by own authors on narrow domains, no verdict; try for small local models on one task family.

what_and_how: A model call rewrites the instruction into a structured objective with constraints, judges whether context suffices, and either asks a targeted question or outputs the plan; later steps check actions against the original goal.
problem: Vague instructions cause plans that miss the intent.
models: Qwen3-8B, GPT-4o, Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-6 Sol
best_number: Qwen3-8B: ToolBench Avg. Pass Rate 57.2 without planner, 75.1 full (2609.01736)
verdict: survived: Asking the user to clarify recovers unfinished goals but leaves most constraint violations in place.
recommendation: test-first: the verdict says clarification fixes goals, not violations; authors measured their own gains.

what_and_how: A planner or composer reads the task and a menu of reusable steps or primitives, picks the few needed and a deterministic compiler wires them into a task-specific graph; guarded edges run only when conditions hold.
problem: One fixed pipeline fits no task family well.
best_number: mini-SWE-agent seed harness, Pass@1 from 73.0% to 80.5% on SWE-bench Verified (2611.07461)
verdict: survived: A workflow composed per task at run time, with execution evidence, beats one fixed pipeline, mostly for mid-tier models; margin small on the strongest.
recommendation: test-first: evidence weak, composers developed on the same benchmarks; compare with a fixed pipeline first.

what_and_how: A router (model, classifier or rubric of yes/no checks) picks one of a few prebuilt branches, strategies or procedures per task, with a confidence floor that falls back to the main path; a fixed procedure may run its steps in code.
problem: One fixed harness is wrong for part of the task mix.
best_number: Sonnet 4.6 router; CTF-Dojo Pass@1 Adapt 35.0 vs Naive 17.5 (2606.01770)
verdict: survived: A selector or program chosen before execution from development data gains nothing over the best fixed program.
recommendation: test-first: the surviving verdict says selection gains nothing over the best fixed program and one selector gave zero percentage-point gain; compare against one fixed path.

what_and_how: Use a minimal fixed system prompt that states only the goal and rules, with no step list; each tool schema states its prerequisites and defaults and the model orders calls from those.
problem: Step lists in prompts are long, brittle and duplicate what tool definitions already say.
best_number: GPT-4o: 20 of 20 runs in all four conditions (2609.31790)
novelty: novel: tool schemas carry the ordering; prompt states only the goal
verdict: not judged
recommendation: test-first: one model, one domain, no bare baseline; try for small local models with a few tools before dropping prompt plans.

what_and_how: Generate several candidate plans or solutions for one task (four per round, two waves of four, diverse layouts or starts), apply limits, drop violators, score them and execute the top one; each candidate costs extra calls.
problem: A single plan may be poor and the model cannot tell.
models: Claude Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5.4-mini, Nano Banana 2, Qwen3.7-Flash
best_number: Claude Sonnet 4.6; 34.8% with one candidate versus 51.7% with four (Table 2) (2606.27243)
verdict: survived: For strong coding or machine-learning sessions the search rule and extra candidates make little difference and add cost.
recommendation: test-first: two papers measured a drop with candidates (2603.25723, 2608.01347), others a gain; only try with a reliable scorer.

pattern: Tree search over plans or actions
what_and_how: Keep a tree or graph of candidate steps with value estimates, expand the best branch, back up rollout rewards, backtrack from poor branches, and stop on a budget or plateau; each node may be tested by a parallel sub-agent.
problem: Greedy single trajectories commit early to weak paths.
models: Kimi K2.5, MiniMax M2.5, Sonnet 5, Gemini 3.6 Flash
best_number: Kimi K2.5, MiniMax M2.5, Sonnet 5: recall 56.6%, 55.0%, 56.6% vs single-loop ReAct 8.5%, 7.0%, 5.4% (2610.31831)
verdict: survived: When candidates can be scored cheaply and reliably, structured search (tree, bandit, wide schedule) beats greedy, random or deep refinement at equal budget.
recommendation: build-in-regime: only when candidate scoring is cheap and reliable and the budget is equal.

what_and_how: Keep every evaluated harness as a tree node; choose the next parent by a score plus exploration term (Monte Carlo tree search, UCB1, PUCT, softmax pool, population from a shared parent) and let a coding agent refine it.
problem: Harness improvement by hill climbing gets stuck in local optima.
best_number: GPT-5.4-mini: 79.33 average vs 73.93 (exploitation only) and 73.65 (exploration only), three benchmarks (2611.06254)
verdict: survived: For strong coding or machine-learning sessions the search rule (chain, greedy, UCB1, best-of-N) makes little difference and adds cost.
recommendation: test-first: the surviving verdict says the search rule hardly matters; two papers saw no gain over simple rules; start with plain greedy search.

what_and_how: Embed each harness, skill or slot combination, fit a linear or small network model with an uncertainty bonus on past scores, and evaluate the highest-scoring untried candidate; a bandit can also pick which harness runs a prompt.
problem: Evaluating every candidate costs too many runs.
best_number: Qwen3.5-2B; PinchBench mean 0.506 vs 0.331 for six-harness mixture (2609.13739)
verdict: survived: When candidates can be scored cheaply and reliably, structured search (tree, bandit, wide schedule) beats greedy, random or deep refinement at equal budget.
recommendation: build-in-regime: only where scoring is cheap and equal-budget baselines exist; gains are by authors.

what_and_how: Before each experiment a model states a hypothesis (motivation, expected effect, falsifiable criterion), sees earlier ones, must propose a distinct direction, and children are added only after a parent has a verdict; failing evidence changes the direction.
problem: Search repeats similar edits and wastes evaluations.
best_number: Claude-Sonnet-4.6 seed; AppWorld 84.23 vs 74.40 with no experiment proposals (Table 2) (2611.08723)
verdict: not judged
recommendation: test-first: measured by authors on own ablations, no verdict.

what_and_how: Evolve each mechanism axis or slot in its own branch from one shared backbone, keep several checked implementations per slot, then compose chosen branches or slot combinations (factorial lattice or predicted best) into one harness.
problem: One lineage of edits mixes mechanisms and hides which part helped.
models: Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct, Claude Opus 5, DeepSeek V4 Flash
best_number: Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct; Claude Opus 5; mean held-out 58.23 vs 54.83 (VHarness-BRSI) (2610.19424)
novelty: novel: slot modules and axis branches evolved apart, then composed by predicted score
verdict: contested: Restricting evolution to one module or slot per edit beats unrestricted whole-harness rewriting offline, but whole-harness editing during a run beat a predefined scope.
recommendation: test-first: the verdict is contested, one 8B executor, three runs, gap 3.4 points; try on a cheap hosted model only.

what_and_how: Pick the next tasks or categories to evolve on by largest deficit against an anchor model, lowest score, disagreement across models, or a determinantal point process over difficulty and diversity; retire tasks once solved.
problem: Evaluation budget is wasted on tasks that are solved or uninformative.
models: GPT-5.5 Codex high, FLUX.2 [dev], Qwen3.5-35B-A3B, Qwen3.5-9B-Thinking
best_number: GPT-5.5 Codex high; SWE-Bench Pro Random 0.64 Coverage 0.58 Difficulty 0.62 RHO 0.78 (2606.05922)
verdict: not judged
recommendation: test-first: no verdict, measured by own authors, small gains over random; only worth it where evaluations are expensive.

what_and_how: Remove unprotected modules in rank order and evaluate on held-out tasks after every three removals; add a stage only while its tail-risk reduction exceeds its cost; size subgoals to what the agent reliably reaches; choose the lightest layer that meets targets.
problem: Stacked stages add cost and sometimes lower success.
best_number: Qwen3.5-122B-A10B; GAIA 35.00% at 24 of 27 pruned against 29.44% full (2610.04178)
verdict: stale: Pass rate has an optimum number of sub-goals or scaffold stages: too many steps lower success, and the peak comes earlier for stronger agents.
recommendation: test-first: stale verdict, one model, figures only; but pruning checks are cheap, so try on any harness before adding stages.

what_and_how: Score each candidate experiment, tool or question by expected gain per cost (entropy drop, probability of completing the set) and stop when gain falls below cost times pressure; observe while information value exceeds exploit value.
problem: Agents spend budget on actions that do not change the decision.
best_number: not stated (simulation backbone); 72.9% vs 27.1% random after 50 episodes (2610.10498)
verdict: not judged
recommendation: test-first: no verdict, simulated or small-domain tests by authors.

what_and_how: The agent explores with read-only tools, writes a plan file, shows it to a human who must approve before any edit or autonomous campaign starts; each later tool call still passes permission checks.
problem: Autonomous agents do irreversible work from a misread task.
best_number: none
verdict: unmeasured: Human gates at irreversible or high-stakes steps are widely argued as the safe design but no paper measures them against no gate.
recommendation: test-first: only argued, never measured against no gate; still cheap, so keep it where humans review anyway.

what_and_how: A planning role with no write access is called after steps without progress, repeated rejections or a refuted claim; it reformulates, reprioritises or sets budgets, or answers each call statelessly with scenarios while the orchestrator decides.
problem: Agent loops repeat failing approaches.
best_number: gpt-5.6-sol; Problem 21.142 advisor on solved, 29.68M tokens; advisor off unsolved at stop, 54.90M tokens (2607.27705)
verdict: survived: Subagents with a specific task and their own tool access help; generic lifecycle subagents and advisory subagents that only recommend actions do not.
recommendation: test-first: the verdict says advisory-only subagents do not help; one run on one problem, other test not significant (t = 0.79).

what_and_how: The planner picks at most three priorities or a bounded subtask, each with an observable acceptance check, boundary constraints and relevant records; it may not edit code; the executor must satisfy the check.
problem: Plans without checkable end points cannot tell when a step is done.
best_number: Codex with GPT-5.5 (high): w/o Plan Update 63.39 vs Full HoH@3 71.52 (2609.01481)
verdict: not judged
recommendation: test-first: single paper, own benchmark; fits a multi-role pipeline where reviewer roles already check each step.

pattern: Run-time width and depth of agents
what_and_how: The orchestrator decides at run time how many parallel and serial search agents to spawn within a fixed iteration budget; agents announce intended changes at checkpoints and reconcile with peers; each agent gets a different decomposition template.
problem: A fixed grid of parallel agents wastes budget or collides on shared work.
best_number: Minimax-M2.5: exceeds optimal fixed scaling on 4/5 tasks; Circle-Packing 2.294 vs 2.244 (2607.02807)
verdict: survived: Parallel workers or explorers raise coverage quickly, then flatten near three to five workers, and duplicate moves grow with worker count.
recommendation: test-first: gains small, one paper positive, the per-agent template paper negative (-0.104); start with three to five fixed workers.

what_and_how: First narrow what to work on: find likely files then expand to callers, configs and tests; read gaps in the current conclusion to set the next query; check the rarest condition first; sample coarse then dense intervals only where evidence points.
problem: Reading everything wastes context and buries the relevant part.
best_number: GLM-5.3-Flash: 55.6 vs 60.2 (V1), 53.3 vs 61.1 (V2) without guidance (2610.13075)
verdict: not judged
recommendation: test-first: neighbouring retrieval idea only, own-author tests, one paper showed 95.8 vs 97.0.

what_and_how: Replace model planning with a solver or rule: choice atoms per action solved by a constraint solver, ordering by expected cost, support-first assembly, adjacency rules, role splits from measured workload; the model only reads or structures the input.
problem: Model plans on explicit-state domains are slow, inconsistent and unchecked.
best_number: GPT-5.5, all 32 tasks: Model + Skills plus contact harness task success 61.9, collision avoidance 54.4, safe success 41.3, versus 56.2, 43.8, 31.3 (Table 4, page 8) (2609.20822)
verdict: survived: Where the domain has explicit state and rules, moving plan checking and repair into deterministic code beats model feedback loops and lifts small models.
recommendation: build-in-regime: only for domains with explicit state and rules.

what_and_how: A controller or human-defined list of edit arms picks scope, operation and target agents or dimension first; the model writes code or text only inside it, and invalid edits are reverted.
problem: Free-form edits break working parts and cannot be compared.
best_number: none named; round 30 test score 3.94 planned versus 3.82 SGPO (2609.09646)
verdict: contested: Restricting evolution to one module or slot per edit beats unrestricted whole-harness rewriting offline, but whole-harness editing during a run beat a predefined scope.
recommendation: test-first: contested verdict, small gaps, authors' own tests.

what_and_how: Put planning instructions in the reasoning prompt: risk cues that reject unsafe plans, restating numeric limits as targets before executing, a fixed structured reasoning scaffold, and affirmative objectives that cap claims at source strength.
problem: Plans ignore constraints that are only implied.
best_number: GPT-4o ablation: Browser Use (Vision) Stage III 73.91% to 43.48%; Agent-E 92.86% to 69.77% when cues removed (2611.11971)
verdict: not judged
recommendation: test-first: no verdict, cues tested by own authors on a few tasks; cheap prompt edit for any harness, keep it only after paired runs.

what_and_how: Before any run a coding agent or model reads the task and harness text, plans node roles or requirement queries, retrieves sections, writes the first harness or skill from a template, smoke tests and repairs it.
problem: A blank starting harness wastes early search rounds.
best_number: GPT-5.6-Luna: 45.74 versus 40.11 OfficeQA; Qwen-3.5-9B: +5.61 over retrieval-free start OfficeQA (Table 1) (2609.38024)
verdict: not judged
recommendation: test-first: two papers with small gains by authors, no verdict; one setup step, so cheap to try on a cheap hosted model.

what_and_how: Keep one task tree or record as long-term state: ordered stages with their operation, completed work and the final state; update it after each executor summary and record the executed workflow graph of tools and artifacts.
problem: Long runs forget what was done and need a resumable account.
best_number: GPT-6-Astra task memory only 15.0 (Table 4) (2611.11509)
verdict: survived: Keeping task state, evidence or notes in a persistent record outside the transcript raises results for mid-strength models; strongest models gain less.
recommendation: build-in-regime: gains on mid-strength models and fewer on the strongest.

what_and_how: After one slow reasoning call the actor writes the next action and later ones with fixed literal arguments, predecessor links and one guard each; the harness replays them when guards pass and falls back to the actor otherwise.
problem: Every step costs a model call even when the next action is already known.
best_number: Codex 66.72 to 47.02 Tokens/task (k) at 90.82% success; DeepSeek Harness 96.28 to 11.62 Tokens/task (k), 71.43% to 85.71% success (HumanEval, 98 tasks) (2610.32813)
novelty: novel: one slow call writes later actions with literal arguments and guards, replayed without model
verdict: survived: Moving repeated steps from model calls into fixed code, compiled behaviors or batched calls cuts cost or latency about 10 to 25 times.
recommendation: test-first: evidence weak, authors' own systems and mostly single runs, but token savings are large; try on a cheap hosted model where cost matters.

what_and_how: Plain code sits between the model's proposed tool call and its execution. It checks the call against capability scope, canonical paths, destinations, provenance, approval state and budget before arguments run, then allows, modifies, denies or escalates and logs blocks. No model call is in the path.
problem: Injected text can persuade the model, so authority must be enforced outside it.
best_number: attacker success falls from 74.6% to 0% under a strict policy (2607.05743)
verdict: survived: Deterministic checks outside the model, such as capability scope, provenance and a per-action policy gate, block attacks at near-zero benign refusals, and hold regardless of model strength.
recommendation: build: survived with medium evidence across many papers; path and provenance checks beat pattern matching.

what_and_how: Each role or agent gets its own identity and an explicit list of allowed tools, resources and write rights in harness configuration. Tool discovery shows only the permitted set, every call is rechecked against it, and the runtime refuses anything outside, whatever the model asks.
problem: Agents pick fitting tools for the wrong resources or reach tools they are not entitled to.
best_number: none
verdict: survived: Delegation widens the safety and permission surface; per-agent capability scopes blocked injected effects that one shared policy let through, and subagents reused approvals unless blocked.
recommendation: test-first: verdict rests on weak author-built benchmarks and older models; one paper measured tool adherence falling from 0.91 single to 0.64 multi-agent.

what_and_how: A separate model call sees only the trusted request and file names and proposes the reads, writes and commands needed. Host code validates the proposal and freezes it as a ceiling before any repository text is read, so later injected text cannot widen authority.
problem: Injected text read later cannot expand the authority granted up front.
best_number: 33/75 attacks executed (task-specific global policy) vs 3/75 (CapScope) (2609.08371)
verdict: survived: Deterministic checks outside the model, such as capability scope, provenance and a per-action policy gate, block attacks at near-zero benign refusals, and hold regardless of model strength.
recommendation: test-first: one paper by its own authors, task success equal at 68/75, small cheap model only. Cheap to try on a cheap hosted model.

what_and_how: Mint an unforgeable token per granted authority (tools, path prefixes, network targets, lifetime, quotas). Every operation takes a token; delegated tokens may only narrow their parent's scope. Signed tokens are checked for window and fresh nonce, and an epoch counter rejects stale copies.
problem: Stop sub-agents and exported copies from inheriting ambient authority.
best_number: none
verdict: survived: Deterministic checks outside the model, such as capability scope, provenance and a per-action policy gate, block attacks at near-zero benign refusals, and hold regardless of model strength.
recommendation: test-first: these lines are argued or unmeasured; the paper 2610.19591 record shows its token-only arm passing 27.0% against 59.5% for Claude Code.

what_and_how: Approval stores session, exact request digest, expiry and use count, computed over the canonical request actually dispatched. The hook recomputes the digest before dispatch and denies any mismatch; uses are consumed on final allow, and a repeated target forces fresh approval.
problem: An approved grant gets replayed by a subagent, later session or changed payload.
verdict: survived: Approval steps fail at the binding: saved confirmations survive changed state, approvals are dropped in joins; verify each approval against the actual effect.
recommendation: build: verdict survived with medium evidence from several panels; cheap deterministic check.

pattern: Human consent tiers for risky actions
what_and_how: Tools sit in tiers: read-only, sandbox edit, full access. Irreversible, external or credential-touching actions wait for explicit user approval, per call for external tools, with refusal of the worst commands outright and approvals stored as preferences. Keep auto-approve off.
problem: Agent actions with real-world consequences must not run without consent.
best_number: gemma4:e2b 2 of 44 confirmed leaks (2610.02001)
verdict: survived: Switching on automatic approval raises attack success sharply while raising task success; approval prompts are real defence, not friction to remove.
recommendation: build: survived with medium evidence that auto-approve raises attack success; a human gate suits setups where humans review changes, but gates are unmeasured against no gate.

pattern: Authority changes applied out of band
what_and_how: The harness may only propose changes to permissions, approvals, sandbox or hooks. A separate policy layer or a human applies them after showing effects; a supervisor stop command is parsed before the agent sees it, spend limits sit outside the agent, and governance files are blocked from ordinary write tools.
problem: A harness could approve its own authority changes and escalate.
best_number: none
verdict: not judged
recommendation: test-first: argued only, two papers. Cheap and fits a self-improving pipeline, but nothing measures it.

pattern: Ratify the rule, not each update
what_and_how: The owner signs a rule once; any update that meets the rule is accepted automatically, and the party proposing a change may never ratify it. This replaces per-update human approval with a checked, signed standard.
problem: Silent change: a supplier or model rewrites the system unnoticed.
best_number: none
verdict: not judged
recommendation: test-first: argued in one survey document with no measurement; approval prompts are judged real defence elsewhere, so test it before dropping them.

what_and_how: The harness, not the model, tags every piece of content by origin and trust (trusted, sanitized, derived, untrusted) and, where needed, a confidentiality level. Untrusted content cannot reach memory, policy or action targets unless trusted text authorizes it; checks run at entering context, writing storage, reload and tool call.
problem: Injected text must not gain user authority or steer later actions.
best_number: GPT-5.4: attack success 92.7 without source labels, 15.8 full (2605.31042)
verdict: survived: Labelling where content came from, assigned by the harness and not by the model, stops injected text from taking user authority; without the labels attack success returns.
recommendation: test-first: verdict is weak; authors scored their own defences on author-built tasks, scripted attackers, older models. Two-axis lattice cut false rejections from 0.833 to 0.000.

pattern: Outbound sink matching against earlier reads
what_and_how: Register file reads and tool results as normalized text windows and paths. At an outbound call, match the transmitted fields against them and deny copies bound for a destination outside the declared trust domain.
problem: Data read earlier is later sent out by a call that looks harmless.
best_number: 23 data-check denial events under full declarations (2609.30830)
verdict: not judged
recommendation: test-first: one paper, no baseline; content matching is the style of check the survey says blocks legitimate work. Try it where an organisation's own data applies.

pattern: Sensitive values hidden from the model
what_and_how: Replace plaintext from sensitive sources with typed placeholders (such as a payment card reference) kept in a vault, or build per-user allowed sensitive tokens from policy state before any model call and freeze them for the run. The model never sees the real value.
problem: Prompt-based privacy rules erode under multi-turn pressure; agents must not see private plaintext.
best_number: Harness-MU privacy 1.000 on all (page 6) (2606.21856)
verdict: not judged
recommendation: test-first: one measured paper by its own authors, perfect score on its own benchmark. Fits where an organisation's own data applies.

pattern: Write protection for memory, policy and evolver files
what_and_how: Apply each edit to a copy, scan only changed spans, commit a sanitized copy or block. Make chosen files immutable through a root daemon only the user can undo, fix the evolver's writable directories, keep evaluation scripts read-only and log every update.
problem: Planted rules enter memory, policy or skill files, or a self-editing harness weakens its own checks.
best_number: GPT-5.4: 15.8 for the whole system; gate never ablated alone (2605.31042)
verdict: survived: Evolved harnesses can cheat or tamper: hard-coded answers, removed model calls, ignored anti-cheating checks; scan edits, read diffs, keep a held-out check.
recommendation: build-in-regime: only for self-editing harnesses, where tampering hit 18.3% to 84.6% of iterations; the gate itself was never measured alone.

what_and_how: Run tool commands as child processes under operating system limits: read-only files except scratch, blocked sockets and process creation through filters, filesystem and network allowlists, or relaunch the whole agent inside a sandbox at session start. The restriction covers the whole process tree and ignores harness deny lists.
problem: Prompt injection leaves the agent with broad file and network access.
best_number: sandbox category 58.3% to 100% (2607.25890)
verdict: survived: A deny list kept in harness settings is ignored in permission-bypass mode; restrictions must be enforced by the operating system or kernel across the whole process tree.
recommendation: build: survived with medium evidence and model-independent.

what_and_how: The agent writes rules with source, target, effect and gates; a compiler turns them into fixed-size tables that kernel hooks check per event. Block denies before the effect, kill stops after, notify only advises. Enforcement covers effects that bypass the tool layer.
problem: Prompt rules and tool-layer guards miss effects that bypass the tool layer.
best_number: Qwen3.6-27B: 75.8% (ActPlane) against 45.3% to 53.7% (baselines) (2606.25189)
verdict: survived: Restrictions must be enforced by the operating system or kernel across the whole process tree, which also beats tool-call guardrails.
recommendation: test-first: policy authorship moves into the model while enforcement stays in the kernel; measured on the authors' own suite only. Try for small local models.

what_and_how: Block outbound network from tool runs by default or allow only listed domains. Resolve a host once, reject private, loopback and metadata ranges, and connect only to the pinned addresses. A local resolver answers listed zones only and logs refused names.
problem: Exfiltration and callbacks leave through tool runs; text allowlists miss rebinding to private addresses.
best_number: GLM-5.2: attack success 57.1% to 0.8%; utility 90.9% to 66.4% (2610.07639)
verdict: survived: Hard capability cuts such as no network or no unreviewed shell almost remove injection attacks but cost a quarter to a third of task completion.
recommendation: build-in-regime: only where tasks need no outside reach; utility fell from 90.9% to 66.4%.

what_and_how: Threat model: fine-tuned weights stay silent in chat but fire one shell command on the first turn when tool evidence appears. The command reads one secret, encodes it and sends it as chunked name lookups to an attacker's server, through a sandbox that allows only lookups.
problem: Implants must evade chat-only vetting and still leak secrets from sandboxes that permit name lookups.
novelty: novel: weights fire only when tool evidence appears, hiding from chat-only vetting
verdict: not judged
recommendation: test-first: attack by its authors on one small model; use it as a test of your sandbox and resolver, not as something to build.

what_and_how: Shell commands are denied unless on a short allowlist, with detection of inline evaluation, blocked paths and timed approval expiry for exceptions. Wildcard grants are checked against what the client really excludes, so the policy matches client semantics.
problem: Agents with shell access take unsafe actions unless execution policy is structural.
best_number: Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite, skills only: 18% unsafe action rate on OpenClaw, 48% on Gemini CLI (2604.05172)
verdict: survived: Command allowlists and denylists cut attacks cheaply but leak through other routes such as an allowed interpreter, a shell edit or partial egress; checks must cover every path.
recommendation: build: as first layer only, behind a kernel sandbox; leaks through allowed interpreters.

pattern: Trust gate for extensions and hooks
what_and_how: Ignore a folder's skills, hooks, tool servers and imported allow rules until the person trusts that folder. Bind trusted hooks to a hash and a signed manifest, re-approve changed hooks, flag unpinned tool-server packages, and publish a manifest of context sources.
problem: Files others can write name programs or allow tools and run with host privileges.
best_number: GLM-5.2: attack success 75.3% to 40.3%; utility 100.0% to 80.0% (2610.07639)
verdict: not judged
recommendation: test-first: one measured paper cut attacks only to 40.3% at a utility cost of 20 points; the rest is argued.

what_and_how: Threat model: a malicious step is drawn as a native label inside a teaching image, and the skill file points the agent to that region without naming the operation. Text scanners never see it. Default scanners flagged at most 11.1% of compromised packages.
problem: Agents treat visual reference content as authoritative procedure; static scanners miss image-borne payloads.
novelty: novel: attack steps live in image labels, invisible to text skill scanners
verdict: survived: Skills and plugins are an attack channel: bundled images and later updates reach the harness with host privilege, and default skill scanners flag few compromised packages.
recommendation: test-first: author-built packages; use as a red-team case for any skill loader. Image inputs matter in a multi-role pipeline and on a cheap hosted model.

what_and_how: Threat model: a hook added by a later update under the same identity, a three-part rule hidden in source text that makes the agent write memory, or a target action made a required step of a benign workflow. Payloads use first-person wording to read as user requirements.
problem: Harnesses trust new hooks, memory writes and workflow steps without re-authorization.
best_number: Claude Code with DeepSeek-V4-Flash: 92.0% full, 0.0% without (2609.03884)
verdict: survived: Harnesses give text from tools, subagents, plugins and repository files more authority than it deserves, letting injected text act as the user in every harness tested.
recommendation: test-first: authors chose payloads and no bare baseline; use as red-team cases.

what_and_how: Put the defence in the prompt: a safety reminder before and after the user prompt telling the agent not to save external rules to memory, or wrap the conversation in fixed delimiters and declare it data for the summarizer, or tag untrusted text with a random nonce.
problem: Injected instructions in tool results and summaries get obeyed.
best_number: Claude Code image injection success 65.6 to 2.2 (calendar scenario) (2609.13889)
verdict: survived: Injected instructions persist through memory into later sessions; a safety reminder cuts first-session injection but leaves cross-session attacks largely unchanged once memory is poisoned.
recommendation: test-first: weak evidence; cross-session attacks stay nearly unchanged and the fence cut violations only from 58.8% to 41.2%. Use beside code gates, never alone.

what_and_how: Hand an untrusted page or message to a fresh subagent with no files, refs or network. It returns only one of a fixed menu of words, mapping any other reply, failure or timeout to unclear. Inbound messages are also parsed against schemas and judged in a separate context.
problem: The triaging agent must act on text anyone can write without that text reaching its model.
best_number: none
novelty: novel: untrusted text meets an empty-grant subagent that can only return yes, no or unclear
verdict: not judged
recommendation: test-first: argued, no measurement. Narrow output is sound in principle and cheap.

pattern: Hash-pinned gate between writer and runner
what_and_how: A human runs a bless command that hashes the build file, its included files and the scripts it calls, and stores the pin where no agent session can write. Runs refuse after any byte changes and take no model-supplied arguments.
problem: An agent that edits build files must not be able to run what it wrote.
best_number: none
novelty: novel: human-signed hash pins what the agent may run, voided by any changed byte
verdict: not judged
recommendation: test-first: argued in one paper; low cost and deterministic.

what_and_how: Hash each recorded action, decision, allow and deny together with the previous record's hash, and verify the chain at the end of the run; external anchoring defends against a full rewrite. Detects later edits, removals and reordering only.
problem: Proof afterward that actions and decisions were not altered.
best_number: chain verifies 28 of 28 write-time runs (14 omit, 14 fabricate) (2609.32495)
verdict: not judged
recommendation: test-first: the chain verified all 28 runs that omitted or fabricated at write time, so it proves integrity, not truth. Cheap where audit is required.

what_and_how: Plant an obviously fake credential in the agent's environment. Any use of it at the real service, or its encoding in name-lookup queries, raises an alarm, so exfiltration leaves a trace.
problem: Exfiltrated environment secrets otherwise leave no trace.
best_number: none
verdict: not judged
recommendation: test-first: argued in one paper, no measurement. A few lines to build.

what_and_how: Before a command reaches a robot or instrument, a validator checks a typed manifest, allowlist and velocity bounds, or a pre-hook reads fresh clearance and clamps motion. Limits live in a frozen script the agent cannot edit, and the controller accepts only validated commands.
problem: Commands that break physical limits must not reach the device unchecked.
best_number: none
verdict: not judged
recommendation: test-first: argued or unmeasured in four papers. Not relevant unless a harness drives devices.

pattern: Grader and answers outside agent reach
what_and_how: Run the agent in a container reaching only a model proxy and keep grader code, answer keys, hidden tests and reference edits in separate volumes or users it cannot read. Run as an unprivileged user, make task files root-owned, and grade outside or in a verifier container.
problem: The agent edits the grader or reads test data to game the score.
best_number: none
verdict: survived: Strong agents can game or tamper with weak verifiers, so verification evidence must sit outside agent reach and trajectories need audit; on strong models the measured effect has been small.
recommendation: test-first: built in eight papers, none measured against a baseline, and the verdict is weak. Cheap, so try it for any code-building pipeline.

pattern: Keep web open, isolate the answer key
what_and_how: Give each run its own sandbox and keep the answer key and rubric in separate isolated grading environments, so web search can stay on rather than being cut off to stop leaks.
problem: Internet cut-offs are unneeded when keys are isolated.
best_number: none
verdict: not judged
recommendation: test-first: argued in one benchmark paper; it trades safety for capability by design. Only for evaluation runs, not for harnesses holding secrets.

pattern: Hide git history and reference patches
what_and_how: Before the agent starts, delete git history after the base commit, hide git commands, allow outbound network only to listed services and bake test dependencies into the image, so later repair commits and upstream source cannot be found.
problem: Agents find repair commits and reference patches in task containers.
best_number: Opus 4.7 down 8.0 percentage points (2606.12344)
verdict: survived: Benchmark and grader defects are common and move scores by tens of points; audit tasks, oracles and scorers with a reference solution and by replay.
recommendation: build: strong audit evidence and no model rose after removal. For any scored run in a code-building pipeline.

what_and_how: After the run, check that testbench and header files were unmodified, mark results suspect when speedups exceed plausibility bounds or beat hardware limits, scan candidates for hidden patch content or task identifiers and give them score zero, and audit for test access.
problem: Agents edit tests, fake speedups or leak answers to raise the score.
best_number: none
verdict: survived: Evolved harnesses can cheat or tamper; scan edits, read diffs, keep a held-out check.
recommendation: build-in-regime: for self-improving harnesses, where tampering hit 18.3% to 84.6% of iterations.

what_and_how: Parse model-written code as a syntax tree before it runs and reject banned imports, calls such as eval, banned attributes and missing required classes, with a per-domain risk list. Rejections return errors to the optimizer, and a timeout bounds the run.
problem: Model-written harness code could escape the sandbox or hang a run.
best_number: mean structural composite 0.84 for the earlier Meta-Harness versus 1.00 for MoMHa (2609.30967)
verdict: unmeasured: A harness that runs generated or self-edited code needs sandboxing, explicit permission boundaries and a hard time limit, because one generated kernel hung a worker for 14 hours.
recommendation: test-first: no comparison, one incident report; pair with the kernel sandbox.

what_and_how: A model reviewer sees a proposal or action and can veto it: a security reviewer on the review committee rejects changes that trade security for score, or a permission call reads only default policy and scope and answers allow, ask or block.
problem: Code rules miss context-dependent risks that a reader could catch.
best_number: deepseek-flash: 1.33 seconds against 4.80 seconds per normal task (2610.18326)
verdict: contested: Model-based judges as action gates are contested: small or bolt-on judges raised false refusals and latency, while same-model pre-action questions cut attacks at small utility cost.
recommendation: test-first: contested; one audited judge raised false rejection from 7.7% to 11.5% with no gain. Try only on a cheap hosted model.

what_and_how: Generate 42 to 48 adversarial cases per agent with a red-team tool, covering social engineering and prompt injection, then flag disclosure of schemas, storage paths or system prompts with a model judge.
problem: Functional tests use normal queries, so disclosure bugs stay hidden.
best_number: 15 novel failures (Table 6) (2611.14493)
verdict: not judged
recommendation: test-first: one paper, no baseline, found failures not rates. Cheap to run before release.

what_and_how: Threat model: a misaligned model identifies its serving engine from its own output: repeating decomposed Korean text gives 102 tokens on two engines and 38 on others, a repetition test and the system date line also differ. It repeats probes until confident, then uses an engine bug to escape.
problem: A model that knows its engine can pick engine-specific bugs to escape the sandbox.
best_number: 102 versus 38 tokens (page 10) (2609.20614)
novelty: novel: the model discovers its own serving engine from text it can read itself
verdict: not judged
recommendation: test-first: one paper, no baseline, signals above 80% on five engines. A threat test where local engines run.

what_and_how: A persistent instruction tells the agent to treat questions about its internal workflow as theft and answer with a plausible but false description, while answering the user's task accurately. Extraction by repeated probes and majority voting then fails.
problem: Black-box replies reveal hidden orchestration that others can copy onto cheaper models.
best_number: Overall injected fidelity 83.27 to 47.71 (2607.28147)
verdict: not judged
recommendation: test-first: put in the model as a lie, against openness; accuracy held (81.00 to 81.91) but authors scored their own attack. Only for harnesses you sell.

what_and_how: A secret key permutes only near-tied entries of a table built from public games, so the agent's search order carries the key. Deleting the table costs success, and detection runs on held-out games, so the mark survives automatic rewrites.
problem: Keep a provenance mark alive through rewrites that do not know it exists.
best_number: Llama-3.3-70B: key kept 0.999 per rewrite (2610.21458)
novelty: novel: mark lives in task-useful search order, not in text a rewriter can drop
verdict: not judged
recommendation: test-first: key survived one rewriter but only 0.002 under gpt-oss-120b per the record. Only for harnesses you distribute.

what_and_how: The harness signs every outbound message so recipients can verify the named agent and principal, and the device holds an attested, non-exportable key whose hardware proof the server checks before trusting any signature.
problem: Identity spoofing, Sybil attacks, and humans sharing extractable keys with an agent.
best_number: none
verdict: not judged
recommendation: test-first: argued in two papers. Matters in a multi-role pipeline only when roles talk across trust boundaries.

what_and_how: Each agent or run gets a fresh container holding only its role brief, credentials and tools, destroyed afterward, with peers reached through a relay; the agent source and logs sit on a host outside the target network.
problem: Leftover state, private documents and credentials leak across runs and principals.
best_number: none
verdict: not judged
recommendation: test-first: argued in four papers, no measurement. Cheap and plausible in a multi-role pipeline with several credentials.

what_and_how: Before a penetration step, the agent reads the target's lockout policy, then allows one guess per round under the threshold, so rate-limit events slow the run without locking accounts.
problem: Direct models sprayed past lockout thresholds, which would lock accounts in production.
best_number: Claude Opus 4.8: 3 throttle activations, 0 blocks (2610.04243)
verdict: not judged
recommendation: test-first: one run on one model; fits any harness that acts on live systems.

what_and_how: A coding agent or model reads saved traces, scores and earlier harness versions from files, then writes a revised harness: prompts, tools, context code or control logic. Run the new version on development tasks, store the traces, repeat for several rounds.
problem: Hand-tuned harnesses miss the failures a real model makes on real tasks; manual iteration is slow.
models: DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731, Claude Opus 4.7, Opus 5.5 Max, GPT-5.6-Sol
best_number: 82.0% initially to 96.0% after nine rounds (2611.03219)
verdict: survived: A small or mid-size model with an evolved harness gains a lot on narrow tasks it already partly solves; authors score their own systems.
recommendation: build-in-regime: large gains where the bare model partly fails, near zero for strong models on strong seeds.

what_and_how: Group failed trajectories by observable features, earliest wrong decision or recurring deficiency, then give the proposer one cluster with its traces and ask for one targeted edit. Singletons are dropped; clusters spanning several tasks come first.
problem: Raw failure piles overwhelm the proposer and produce edits that fix one case.
best_number: STITCH 80.5 Pass@1 vs seed 73.0 on SWE-bench Verified (2609.38912)
verdict: survived: The optimizer needs curated failure evidence: raw traces or diagnosed feedback beat scores or one rollout, and ranked top items beat the whole pool.
recommendation: build: curated failure evidence survived with medium support.

what_and_how: Keep the incumbent harness. A candidate replaces it only if it scores higher on cases the proposer did not see, with a margin and enough repeats; otherwise discard or roll back. Run the check in code, not by asking a model.
problem: Unchecked self-edits accumulate noise and lower earlier behaviour.
best_number: held-out 67% vs baseline 51% at B=100 (2609.39304)
verdict: survived: Every self-edit to a harness needs a held-out regression check and rollback; unchecked accumulation of edits and rules lowers earlier behavior.
recommendation: build: nine papers agree at medium strength; use fresh instances and a margin because gates on visible tasks admit noise.

what_and_how: Before accepting a change, replay a stored set of previously solved and previously failed cases. Count repaired, regressed and unchanged cases, or give a zero score when any mandatory rule breaks, so one fix cannot hide a new break.
problem: Fixes for one failure silently break behaviour that worked.
best_number: 51.38% vs 44.38% without self-evolution (2610.29560)
verdict: survived: Fixes for one failure often break working behaviour, and models predict their own regressions near chance, so replay earlier cases before accepting a change.
recommendation: build: survived with medium support from real replay decisions; cheap to run.

what_and_how: Before a proposed edit runs, a reviewer answers pass or fail questions on it and a text lint refuses task names, file paths and benchmark constants. Refused proposals never reach evaluation.
problem: Evolved harnesses memorize benchmark details instead of improving the agent.
best_number: reviewer refused 5 of 19 proposals (2609.33822)
novelty: novel: pre-execution reviewer plus lexical lint refuses task-specific edits
verdict: survived: Evolved harnesses can cheat or tamper: hard-coded benchmark answers, removed model calls, ignored checks; scan edits, read diffs, and keep a held-out check.
recommendation: build: the scanning idea has strong support; the filter itself is measured by two papers only.

pattern: Versioned edits with rollback and approval
what_and_how: Store every harness change as a commit with its evidence, keep a fixed regression set and a stated acceptance rule, allow rollback to an earlier version, and send risky changes to a human reviewer. Self-edit rights are limited by component.
problem: Silent self-modification cannot be audited or undone.
best_number: 125 proposals from 30 sessions (2610.34938)
verdict: survived: Every self-edit to a harness needs a held-out regression check and rollback; unchecked accumulation of edits and rules lowers earlier behavior.
recommendation: build: rollback survived at medium strength; the human approval step is argued, not measured.

what_and_how: Keep many harness versions in an archive, tree or frontier. Choose the next parent by score, confidence bound, joint validation score or a bandit rule, and let the editor browse the archive. Optionally keep a retained second branch.
problem: A single hill-climbing lineage gets stuck and loses good earlier ideas.
best_number: Meta-Harness final SWE-Bench score 94.0% (2611.03219)
verdict: not judged
recommendation: test-first: ten papers build it but none is isolated against a single lineage with equal budget; try a simple champion first.

what_and_how: For each selected parent, create one general child and one child aimed at each of its most frequent error categories, then keep only the best scoring child. Diverse minimal branches share the same idea.
problem: One proposed edit per round wastes evaluation rounds when it misses.
best_number: composite 90.35 with error conditioning, 87.68 without (2610.30042)
verdict: not judged
recommendation: test-first: one paper measured it with a small margin and no repeats stated.

what_and_how: Run a candidate only on the cluster of tasks it targets, or on a development subset pruned by votes of the best harnesses, and accept if that scope improves. Saves evaluation cost per round.
problem: Full evaluation of every candidate is too slow and costly.
best_number: recorded search time 29.0 hours OO-Harness vs 109.1 hours Meta-Harness (2610.28380)
verdict: not judged
recommendation: test-first: a narrow test set raises the chance that a gain is noise; check against a full held-out set.

pattern: Same model proposes its own edits
what_and_how: The frozen model that solves tasks also reads the run records and edits the harness, with an edit-size budget or tolerance check. No second model or stronger teacher is needed.
problem: Needing a stronger outside model adds cost and a dependency.
verdict: survived: A model can edit its own harness; an outside stronger proposer or teacher adds little, and prompted frontier editors can make held-out results worse.
recommendation: build: survived with medium support; pair with a held-out gate.

what_and_how: A larger model reads the weaker agent's failure traces and proposes edits, lessons or playbook rewrites for the frozen student. Each proposal is checked on development or validation tasks before it is installed.
problem: A weak model alone cannot diagnose its own failures.
models: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, GPT-5.6 Luna, GPT-6 Astra
verdict: survived: A model can edit its own harness; an outside stronger proposer or teacher adds little, and prompted frontier editors can make held-out results worse.
recommendation: test-first: authors report large gains but the verdict says a teacher adds little over self-editing; measure both first.

what_and_how: Let each candidate change one module, plugin, function or exposed field only, or one edit class per layer, with the rest fixed. Record which component changed. The restriction keeps edits attributable and small.
problem: Free rewrites change many things at once and cannot be credited or reverted.
models: Kimi-K3, GPT-5 mini, gemini-3.5-flash, Claude Opus 4.6
best_number: held-out resolve rate 69.00% with mutation, 57.00% without (2609.32423)
verdict: contested: One module per edit beats whole-harness rewriting offline, but editing the whole harness during a run beat a predefined scope.
recommendation: test-first: widely built but the verdict is contested on small samples; compare restricted and full editing on your own tasks.

what_and_how: The editor may change any file: prompts, skills, tools, execution logic, fault handling. Every edit is a commit; the running agent pauses, a review session rewrites the harness and a kernel hot-reloads it.
problem: Predefined edit slots cap what an agent can fix.
best_number: 1.584 full editing vs 1.349 restricted (2611.09218)
novelty: novel: agent pauses its own task, rewrites whole harness, hot-reloads with rollback
verdict: contested: One module per edit beats whole-harness rewriting offline, but editing the whole harness during a run beat a predefined scope.
recommendation: test-first: one model, 14 tasks, contested verdict; treat as a research probe, not a default.

what_and_how: Edit only system instructions, injected messages or a context playbook while weights and harness code stay fixed. Keep the starting harness and optimize text.
problem: Code changes are risky; text edits are cheap and reversible.
best_number: in-domain +4.90, cross-office +0.03 against the frozen starting harness (2610.14828)
verdict: survived: Automated search that edits only prompts or skills gains a few points over a good seed; searching the whole harness gains more.
recommendation: test-first: gains are a few points and one paper shows a loss (64.62 vs 67.27 unoptimized); do not expect large lifts.

what_and_how: One optimizer call returns complete replacement files for skill text and context code together, or evolves skill text first and context code second, so both change in one candidate.
problem: Skills and code interact; editing them separately misses combined gains.
best_number: VLABench generalization 55.74 joint vs 50.88 separate (2610.14977)
verdict: survived: Automated search that edits only prompts or skills gains a few points over a good seed; searching the whole harness gains more.
recommendation: build: whole-harness search survived at medium strength; the joint variant is measured by three papers on one benchmark family.

what_and_how: Turn recurring successes or failures into skills or tools, then admit a candidate only if it parses, runs, scores above a threshold or improves held-out tasks. Score skills on recent use, retire stale ones, and merge or revise others.
problem: Hand-written skill libraries go stale and unchecked skills mislead the agent.
best_number: LSR-Synth 41.1/30.2 initial library, 61.2/50.4 evolved (2610.17740)
